summary: Brick light on the Barrington shore at the mouth of the Providence River (1828-1868); the oldest surviving keeper's house in Rhode Island is now a private home.

lens.where: transferred to the new Conimicut Point light, 1 November 1868 (LighthouseFriends)

structures.note: Three-story square brick tower, 25 feet (7.6 m) to the lantern (USLHS). Replaced an 1828 freestanding octagonal tower to the west.
The 1828 section is the oldest surviving keeper's dwelling in Rhode Island (NRHP). Enlarged 1856, 1875 and about 1905.

access.note: Private residence. The NRHP form lists accessibility as 'yes, restricted'; the USLHS record says not open to the public.

events.note: First freestanding octagonal tower and the keeper's house, both 1828 (NRHP).
Daniel Wightman, first principal keeper on the roster.
A strong winter storm almost destroyed the seawall; the tower cracked from top to bottom (LighthouseFriends).
Second, square brick tower built to replace the 1828 tower (NRHP; USLHS 1856).
New tower began showing its light on 25 December 1856 (LighthouseFriends).
Two-story wing added to the dwelling (NRHP).
Original fourth-order Fresnel lens, per the USLHS record. LighthouseFriends places the Fresnel lens in the new tower from 1856. See resolved_conflicts.
Light discontinued 1 November 1868 and replaced by an offshore beacon east of Conimicut Point (NRHP; USLHS).
Fresnel lens transferred to the new Conimicut Point light (LighthouseFriends).
Floating ice destroyed the keeper's dwelling at the Conimicut beacon, March 1875; the Nayatt Point dwelling was repaired and reoccupied (NRHP; LighthouseFriends).
Sold at public auction for $4,000 (NRHP); LighthouseFriends names the buyer as Charles H. Merriman.

corrections.proposed: 1856 for the standing tower; the 1828 tower was replaced
corrections.why: The NRHP says the 1856 tower was built to replace the original 1828 freestanding tower, and the USLHS record gives 1856 for the tower.
The NRHP nomination lists ownership as private. Owners' names are not recorded here.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The USLHS record gives the original fourth-order Fresnel lens as installed in 1863. LighthouseFriends says a fourth-order Fresnel lens was used in the new lighthouse of 1856. Both are kept; the lens year needs a primary source (Lighthouse Board report, not in the local corpus).

The NRHP puts the new Conimicut tower and keeper's quarters at 1890. LighthouseFriends says the iron Conimicut tower was finished in 1883. The story gives LighthouseFriends's date and notes the NRHP's.
LighthouseFriends says a dwelling was built on the Conimicut pier in 1873; the NRHP says new quarters were completed in 1874. Both show quarters being built in the early 1870s.
The USLHS record's own optic line is '6 14 inch reflectors, FOURTH ORDER, FRESNEL'. The story quotes that line rather than calling the original optic a lens alone.
The nomination describes the 1856 wing as one-story in its description and as two-story in its significance statement. The story says 'brick wing' only.

notes_for_editor: 1. Keepers: all eight names come from the USLHS roster (NARA registers via the Anderson inventory), whose heading is 'Principal Lighthouse Keeper'; normalised to 'head keeper'. Only Wightman and Davis Perry appear in the prose, and not one has been confirmed against a primary record in this pass. Confirm before any more names go into the story. 2. The Bache 1838 report and the Treasury letter are quoted second-hand, through LighthouseFriends (both public-domain texts, footnoted as quoted there). The originals were not read. LighthouseFriends' own prose is paraphrased in this version; it is copyrighted, so only public-domain passages are quoted. 3. The Lighthouse Board reports before 1891 are not in the local corpus, so the 1828-1868 official record, including the lens year, is unchecked. 4. A search of 1875 Rhode Island newspapers turned up no direct report of the March 1875 ice; that event rests on the NRHP (the ice floe) and LighthouseFriends (the March date). 5. The 1868 excursion report (Pawtucket Gazette and Chronicle, 28 August 1868, p. 2) names a host and a private residence; neither is named in the story. The report was checked against the OCR text. 6. LighthouseFriends is an all-rights-reserved site; the story uses its facts in our own words and quotes only public-domain passages. 7. The owners of the house, private since 1890 and named in the NRHP and LighthouseFriends, are not named in the story. 8. The 'Nayatt' name check: the roster matched the USLHS place by name and position (0.61 km), which is good; no other Nayatt in the state is on the list. 9. Living people: none named. 10. Shape: the story has six chapters at about 1,000 words, which the guide's Moderate row would allow only 2-4 for. Left as written because each chapter has sourced material; the editor may merge.
